To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the second harmonic generation (frequency conversion) from a van der Waals heterostructure of hexagonal boron-nitride is strongly tunable by mechanical rotation, which can be used to control the symmetry of the heterostructure and to enhance the conversion efficiency by stacking multiple crystals.
we demonstrate highly tunable second order optical nonlinearity at the interfaces between van der Waals crystals.

the SHG intensity from bulk hexagonal borne nitride (hBN) crystals can be modulated by more than a factor of 50 by nanomechanically rotating the crystal relative to a fixed optical axis, that the SHG polarization is strongly influenced by moire interface structure, and that stacking multiple hBN crystals with symmetry-broken interfaces leads to enhanced conversion efficiency.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study and application of the nonlinear optical properties of 2D layered crystals.
the development of novel optical materials for nonlinear optics.
the nonlinear optical properties of van der Waals materials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have demonstrated highly tunable second-harmonic generation from nanomechanical stacks of bulk hexagonally boron nitride crystals.

we have shown highly tunable second-harmonic generation (SHG), from nanomechanical rotatable stacks of van der Waals crystals, with a modulation factor of more than fifty, and enhanced conversion efficiencies for bulk crystals by symmetry-broken interface stacking.

the work presented in this article demonstrates a new class of tunable nonlinear optical materials based on vdW heterostructures with controllable twist angle, which enables the design and fabrication of highly tunable nonlinear optics architectures for efficient and scalable nonlinear frequency conversion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we demonstrate highly tunable SHG from nanomechanical rotatable stacks of BN crystals.

we have demonstrated the ability to dynamically control nonlinear optical properties in a single device by mechanical manipulation of twist angles in van der Waal heterostructures, and that this approach provides a powerful platform for the study of fundamental symmetry breaking at buried interfaces.
the twistoptics approach can be used to study fundamental properties at interfaces, such as the symmetry of the moire interface, and the symmetry-broken interface.
The main takeaway from our work is that
twist angle, and thus the presence of inversion symmetry, is an important parameter in determining the nonlinear optical response at a crystal interface.
twistoptics provides a new platform for nonlinear optics, with the ability to tune the nonlinear optical response through mechanical manipulation of the twist angle.
symmetry-broken interfaces in vdW materials can be used to control the optical response in a way that is not possible in bulk materials.
